The digital screen flickers, and my stomach drops.

If you plug a TV and the console into this, the surge load is going to trip the main breaker inside the house instantly. Your mom will know exactly what we're doing the second the lights go out."

I point up to the dilapidated treehouse, then back across the lawn.

"We can't use this garage line. The only way it works without tripping the breaker is if we tap into the closer outdoor outlet... the one directly under the kitchen window. Where your mom is standing right now."

*Just as you grab the heavy plastic plug and reach for the weatherproof outlet box, a flash of neon pink drops from the low porch wall right beside you.*

Maya.

She lands perfectly on the soft mulch in her bright rain boots, a pair of binoculars slung around her neck. I freeze, my hand clamping over my own mouth. She stares down at the thick black extension cord in your hands, looks up at the lit window a few feet above your head, and then smiles with devastating, opportunistic glee.

"I want ten bucks," she whispers, her voice cutting sharply through the humid air. "And prime treehouse access on Saturdays. Both of those right now, or I tap on the glass and ask Mom what you're plugging in."

Maya’s eyes go wide. She silently pockets my cash, shoots you an evil, triumphant little salute, and completely melts backwards into the shadows of the porch.

Before my heart can start beating again, the grinding squeak of the kitchen window sliding open right above our heads freezes the blood in my veins.

"Are you crazy?" I breathe, my glasses sliding down my sweaty nose.

But it's too late. The heavy wooden screen door groans open, followed immediately by the blinding, surgical glare of the backyard security floodlight snapping on. It bathes the side yard in harsh, unforgiving white.

Deliberate footsteps crunch on the gravel path. A tall shadow falls over us. I squeeze my eyes shut, actively praying for the rhododendron bush to just swallow me whole. When I peel one eye open, your mom's sensible orthopedic clogs are planted barely three inches from my nose.

"Leo. Sam." Claire's voice is dangerously even. She looks down at us huddled in the mud like terrified garden gnomes, then slowly traces the path of the thick black extension cord snaking from the kitchen wall, over my sneaker, and out toward the distant oak tree.

My stomach plummets right into the dirt. We are completely caught.

"Would either of you care to explain," she asks, crossing her arms and staring daggers into you, "why you are laying in the mud behind my azaleas, secretly wiring the backyard for municipal power?"

*I curl into a defensive ball, fully expecting your mom to yank the cord out of the wall and ground us both until high school. Instead, when you stand up, covered in wet mulch, and boldly declare that you're old enough to manage the treehouse power yourself, the silence between you two is deafening.*

*Claire doesn't yell. She doesn't reach for the socket. She just stares at you, her sharp eyes registering the dirt smeared across your forehead and the defiant, desperate set of your jaw.*

"Is that so?" she finally says. Her tone is dangerously calm, stripping away whatever fleeting hope I had left. "If you are mature enough to secretly engineer an off-grid electrical project, Leo, then I assume the workspace is up to code. Show me."

*My breath hitches. She’s going inside.*

*Before either of us can protest, she pivots on her orthopedic clogs and marches straight across the lawn. We have no choice but to scramble after her. Moments later, we climb the creaky wooden ladder and spill into the Salvaged Command Center.*

*The cheap LEDs cast a pathetic, cool glow over empty soda cans, stripped copper wires, and the precarious tower of milk crates holding your precious gaming console. The air smells intensely of sawdust and impending doom. Claire stands in the center of the cramped, dusty sanctuary, crossing her arms as she surveys the absolute chaos of our 'independent' setup.*

"Well?" she challenges, glaring down at our exposed daisy-chain of power strips. "Convince me."

You confidently point to a peeling layer of silver duct tape wrapped haphazardly around the cracked surge protector, declaring it a "waterproof thermal seal."

Claire doesn't argue. She doesn't even sigh. She just reaches down, grabs the heavy black line, and pulls.

*Pop.*

The cheap LED strips instantly die. Your gaming console shuts off with a pathetic, descending sequence of chimes. The cramped treehouse is plunged into shadowy, humid twilight, suddenly suffocatingly quiet.

"Duct tape degrades in humidity and traps condensation, Leo," your mom says, her voice echoing in the sudden gloom. She begins methodically coiling our precious extension cord over her forearm with terrifying efficiency. "You didn't run these numbers. Your friend did."

She steps over a milk crate toward the hatch, throwing the heavy coil of wire over her shoulder. "You want real independence? You have until sunset tomorrow. Present a fully grounded, outdoor-rated schematic that actually mitigates water ingress. If you can't, I’m taking the console inside and clearing this treehouse down to the bare floorboards."
